The Survey Descent iteration solves k parallel quadratic subproblems, each centered around one of the k survey points.
The paper proves local linear convergence of Survey Descent when the objective is the maximum of k smooth, strongly convex functions.
Experiments suggest Survey Descent may exhibit linear convergence even on objectives not expressible as the maximum of smooth functions.
The size of the survey, k, is related to the dimension of the subdifferential of the objective at the minimizer.
The gradients of the survey points tend to form a convex hull whose dimension matches the subdifferential dimension.
Survey Descent only requires function and gradient evaluations of the overall objective, not access to the individual component functions.
The paper discusses connections to other multipoint methods like bundle methods and level-bundle methods.
The paper's motivation for Survey Descent includes the 'differentiability of every iterate' behavior observed in many first-order methods on nonsmooth objectives.
The authors suggest that the choice of survey size, k, is an important practical question related to the 'active structure' of the objective at the minimizer.
Figures 1-4 in the paper present experiments demonstrating the linear convergence behavior of Survey Descent on various nonsmooth objectives.
The paper contrasts Survey Descent's theoretical guarantees with the generally sublinear convergence rates proven for other first-order methods on nonsmooth objectives.
The authors note that while Survey Descent is motivated by a 'max-of-smooth' model, the method is broadly applicable beyond objectives with that structure.
The paper discusses connections between the dimensionality of the subdifferential at the minimizer and the behavior of first-order method iterates near the minimizer.
The authors suggest that the availability of a 'workable choice' for the survey size, k, is a major assumption for the development and practical implementation of Survey Descent.
The paper presents empirical heuristics for choosing the survey size k based on the dimensionality of the objective's subdifferential at the minimizer.
